title: The Employee Life Cycle: Every Stage and What Your People Need
summary: Explore the six employee life cycle stages and learn how HR can support employees, manage key handoffs and keep people, roles and assets connected.
body_markdown:
## What is the employee life cycle?


The employee life cycle is the model HR uses to describe each stage of a person’s time with an organization, from first contact as a candidate to the last day of employment. Each stage has its own employee needs, business decisions and records.


## What are the six stages of the employee life cycle?


The six core stages of the employee life cycle are attraction, recruitment, onboarding, development, retention and offboarding. Day-to-day workforce management connects those stages by keeping employee, position, pay, location and assigned-resource records current as work changes.


A life cycle view keeps HR from treating recruiting, onboarding, role changes, development and departure as unrelated transactions. One decision can affect the next stage. A role definition shapes recruiting. Onboarding shapes readiness. Development and mobility affect retention. Offboarding affects knowledge transfer, records, access and company property.


### *1. Attract*


Attraction is the work that happens before a candidate applies. This stage helps organizations define the workforce they need now and in the future, communicate why people should want to work there and build interest among qualified candidates before a role becomes urgent to fill.


For example, according to the Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM), today’s talent seeks to work at organizations that offer[transparent skills road maps](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/news/future-focus-irl-revival-skills-insurance-status-by-access) to support career longevity as roles are redefined, technology evolves and organizations scale.


- **what the employee needs:** a clear view of the opportunity, work, the culture and the value of joining
- **what the organization must decide:** which roles matter most, what skills are needed and how the employer brand should set realistic expectations
- **what information must remain current:** workforce plans, position requirements, job descriptions, compensation ranges, location details and employer messaging
- **what to measure:** qualified candidate interest, source quality, application conversion, talent-pool growth and time from need identification to open requisition


### *2. Recruit*


Recruitment is the role-specific phase of talent acquisition. It turns workforce needs into active hiring steps, including job posting, applicant tracking, screening, interviews, selection and offers. The goal is to move qualified candidates through the process with clear communication and enough structure to support fair, timely hiring decisions.


- **what the employee needs:** timely communication, a fair process, role clarity and an offer that matches the work described
- **what the organization must decide:** selection criteria, interview owners, offer terms, start timing and whether the approved position still matches the business need
- **what information must remain current:** candidate status, requisition details, position data, interview feedback, offer approvals and start-date assumptions
- **what to measure:** time to fill, candidate drop-off, offer acceptance, hiring-manager response time, quality of qualified applicants and accuracy of the handoff into onboarding


### *3. Onboard*


Onboarding turns an accepted offer into a prepared first day. It should give the new employee the records, access, workspace, equipment, expectations and relationships needed to begin.


With Paycom, HR sets the seat and equipment a role needs in Position Management. When a new employee is hired, Asset Management automatically assigns a workspace and tools.


- **what the employee needs:** clear first-day instructions, the right tools, required access, a prepared workspace, role expectations and early manager support
- **what the organization must decide:** who owns each onboarding task, what must be completed before Day 1 and which role, workspace or equipment requirements apply
- **what information must remain current:** employee record, position, manager, location, pay details, required forms, access status and assigned assets
- **what to measure:** task completion, readiness by start date, missing-equipment issues, form completion, time to productivity and early employee feedback


For deeper process guidance, see Paycom’s[HR process automation resource](https://www.paycom.com/resources/blog/hr-process-automation/) and[new-hire checklist](https://www.paycom.com/resources/blog/new-hire-onboarding-checklist/) .


### *4. Develop*


The development stage helps employees build capability as work and career goals change. The talent management process may include goal setting, feedback, performance conversations, learning, coaching and movement into new responsibilities.


- **what the employee needs:** useful feedback, relevant learning, clear goals, manager coaching and a visible path for growth or movement
- **what the organization must decide:** which capabilities matter, how performance will be evaluated, which employees are ready for new responsibilities and what role changes require approval
- **what information must remain current:** goals, feedback, learning history, performance records, position changes, manager changes, pay impacts, workspace assignments and equipment needs
- **what to measure:** goal progress, learning completion, internal mobility, promotion readiness, performance conversation completion and whether approved changes are reflected before they take effect


### *5. Retain*


Retention is the organization’s continuing work to create reasons for capable employees to stay. It includes clear expectations, useful manager support, fair and accurate pay processes, development opportunities, sustainable workloads and confidence that workplace systems work as intended.


If the cost of employee turnover is not part of your company’s budget, consider it. In[Workforce Institute’s 2024 Retention Report](https://info.workinstitute.com/hubfs/2024%20Retention%20Report/Work%20Institute%202024%20Retention%20Report.pdf) , U.S. companies spent nearly $9 billion to replace employees who quit in 2023. Reasons for employees leaving vary, but many are preventable with the right tools to do the work.


- **what the employee needs:** trust, support, workable processes, fair treatment, growth opportunities and confidence that their work is understood
- **what the organization must decide:** which retention risks require action, which roles need succession plans, where manager support is needed and which process issues create avoidable friction
- **what information must remain current:** engagement signals, performance history, compensation data, development plans, succession plans, workload indicators, manager assignments and position history
- **what to measure:** turnover, regretted losses, internal movement, engagement trends, manager effectiveness signals, workload issues and completion of retention or succession actions


### *6. Offboarding*


[Employee offboarding](https://www.paycom.com/resources/blog/employee-offboarding-process-and-checklist/) closes the employment relationship through coordinated pay,[required wage-and-hour record documentation](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/fact-sheets/21-flsa-recordkeeping) , access removal, work handoff and property recovery. It applies to voluntary and involuntary departures.


When an employee leaves, Paycom Asset Management automatically flags the equipment assigned to that person for recovery. HR, IT and the manager work from the same list.


- **what the employee needs:** clear communication, respectful closure, accurate final information and a predictable process for returning property or completing next steps
- **what the organization must decide:** final pay timing, access removal, work handoff ownership, replacement or position decisions, asset recovery steps and documentation requirements
- **what information must remain current:** separation reason, effective date, final pay details, benefits status, access status, assigned assets, equipment condition, handoff notes and audit history
- **what to measure:** completion of offboarding tasks, access removal timing, asset recovery, unresolved exceptions, knowledge-transfer completion and separation documentation accuracy


### *Why does the employee life cycle matter?*


An employee life cycle model helps organizations identify gaps between HR processes that are often managed separately. It can also clarify who owns each handoff, which employee information needs to remain current and what resources must change when a person is hired, promoted, transferred or separated.


## Connecting the employee life cycle: Manage the workforce day to day


The employee life cycle continues between milestone events.[Workforce planning](https://www.paycom.com/resources/blog/workforce-planning/) helps leaders match people and positions to expected work, while day-to-day[workforce management](https://www.paycom.com/resources/blog/what-is-workforce-management/) covers time, schedules, leave, pay inputs, approvals and employee changes.


- **what the employee needs:** accurate time, pay, schedules, approvals, leave balances, manager support and role details that match the work being performed
- **what the organization must decide:** how work will be staffed, who approves changes, when schedule or location changes take effect and which routine changes affect pay, assets or workspace
- **what information must remain current:** employee status, manager, location, schedule, time records, leave, pay inputs, position, workspace and assigned resources
- **what to measure:** payroll accuracy, approval cycle time, schedule coverage, leave trends, change-processing time, manager changes, location changes and downstream updates triggered by workforce changes


## What follows an employee through every stage?


### *Employee records*


Employee changes rarely affect only one HR record. A new hire may need an approved position, workspace, laptop and system access. A transfer may change the employee’s location, manager and equipment requirements. An offboarding event can trigger final-pay tasks, access removal, knowledge transfer and property recovery.


### *Equipment and other assigned resources*


Paycom[Asset Management](https://www.paycom.com/software/asset-management/) connects property, people and workspaces in the same single database used to manage the workforce. An organization can maintain records for items such as laptops, furniture and other equipment, including status, value and location, so the asset assignment stays connected to the employee or workspace across life cycle changes.


### *Positions and workspaces*


[Position Management](https://www.paycom.com/software/position-management/) can define the workspace and equipment requirements associated with a role. Because Position Management and Asset Management operate in Paycom’s single database, approved position changes can support related assignment or recovery workflows. This helps teams keep role requirements, employee changes and company property together.


## How to manage changes across the employee life cycle


An employee can move between managers, positions, locations and pay arrangements without leaving the organization. Each approved change needs a clear effective date and a reliable record.


[Personnel Action Forms](https://www.paycom.com/software/personnel-action-forms/) helps organizations automatically document and route employee changes for approval, producing a personnel record that is retained in the software. Keeping the approved change and its effective date in the employee record can give teams a more reliable basis for handling related position, location and equipment updates. For example, Personnel Action Forms records the effective date of an involuntary termination, and[the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) requires employers to keep those personnel records for one year from that date](https://www.eeoc.gov/employers/recordkeeping-requirements) .

## How to evaluate employee life cycle management software


Employee life cycle management software should preserve continuity. The person’s approved information should not lose context when it passes from recruiting to onboarding, from one role to another or from active work to departure. A single record helps HR, payroll, managers, IT and operations work from the same effective dates and assignments.


When evaluating employee life cycle management software, ask:


- Does candidate information carry forward after hiring?
- Can approved role, manager or location changes remain tied to an effective date?
- Can teams see which equipment is assigned to an employee or workspace?
- Can HR, payroll, IT and operations work from the same approved employee and position information?
- Can authorized users review assignment status and history without reconciling separate records?

## Employee life cycle FAQs


### *How many stages are in the employee life cycle?*


The employee life cycle typically has six stages: attraction, recruitment, onboarding, development, retention and offboarding. Organizations may split or rename stages, but the model should show what employees need and what the organization must decide at each point. Plus, day-to-day workforce management occurs continuously throughout the employee life cycle.


### *What is the difference between the employee life cycle and the employee journey?*


The employee life cycle is the organization’s model of stages and processes. The employee journey is the individual’s experience across those stages, including the moments, interactions and perceptions that shape the relationship with the employer.


### *What is the difference between talent acquisition and recruitment?*


Talent acquisition is an ongoing strategy for attracting and selecting people to meet workforce needs. Recruitment is the more immediate work of filling a specific role. Recruitment sits within talent acquisition, alongside workforce planning, employer positioning and candidate relationship building.


### *How does HR software support the employee life cycle?*


HR software supports the employee life cycle by keeping approved employee information available across hiring, onboarding, role changes, pay, development and offboarding. A single database can reduce rekeying and help teams act from the same employee, position and effective-date records.


### *Who owns the employee life cycle in an organization?*


HR usually leads the employee life cycle model, but ownership is shared. Recruiters, managers, payroll, finance, IT, security and operations each control decisions or resources at different stages. The organization should assign accountable owners without fragmenting the employee record.


### *How does asset management fit into the employee life cycle?*


Paycom’s Asset Management tracks the equipment and workspaces assigned to an employee from onboarding through offboarding. When asset records sit in the same database as employee and position records, a hire, transfer or separation can prompt the matching assignment or recovery step.
